Fatal Fight Over a Game of Cards.
ALMA, Ark., Aug. 25.—At Mountainburg last night Tom Simcoe, David Pope and Frank Lane got into a fight over a game of cards. Lane drew a knife and cut Pope in the abdomen, disemboweling him, and then fatally stabbed Simcoe in the breast. Pope lived only an hour. Simcoe was still alive this morning. At last accounts Lane was in the hands of a mob and is believed to have already been lynched.

C. B. Hawley and L. V. and Cicero Grimes have made a full confession at Globe, Arizona Territory, detailing the circumstances attending the robbery of the stage coach and the murder of the messenger, Andy Hall, and Dr. Vail. Twelve or fifteen out of a mob of one hundred men rushed into a train at Madison, Fla., and riddled with bullets two colored prisoners named Savage and James, who had murdered Frank Patterson on February 8th, 1881, in a room where testimony was being taken on a contested election case. At the time they were killed Savage and James were being taken to Jasper, Fla., where the Supreme Court had ordered them to get a new trial.

The county physician of Newark, N. J., is investigating the death of Thomas McGrath, a wealthy widower, who died with indications of poisoning on Wednesday. His approaching marriage displeased his family, some of whom accompanied him on Tuesday to a lawyer's office, where he made his will.
On that night he suddenly became ill,
and he died early on the next morning.

During a quarrel at cards at Mountainburg, Arkansas, Frank Lane fatally stabbed David Pope and Tom Simcoe. A mob lynched Lane last night.

David Taylor, a saloon keeper, of Paterson, N. J., has been sent to jail to await the result of his wife's injuries. He fractured her skull with a beer glass.

Gideon Morris, of Raleigh, N. C., while intoxicated, so brutally beat and kicked his wife that she died at midnight on Thursday.

Harry Foxall was fatally shot at Montclair, N. J., early yesterday morning, by John Hanlan, who claims that the shooting was accidental.

During a quarrel about peaches at Hillsboro' Station, Md., a man named Atkinson shot another man named Ringold. The latter will probably die.

LATEST NEWS.
Timothy Bailey, the inventor of the knitting machine, has just died at Balliston, N. Y.

Deputy Marshal Young went from Little Rock into the Choctaw nation to secure Jones, the supposed murderer of Dr. Bailey, when the brothers in-law of the accused intercepted him at a lonely spot, left him mortally wounded on the highway and fled with the prisoner.

A number of executions, according to the forms of law and otherwise, took place Friday, Aug. 25, all in the Southern States. At Alken, S. C., Robert Parker was hanged for having poisoned his wife with strychine; at Madison, Fla., William Bryan was hanged for the assassination of Jack Moore; at Newcastle, Del., James Redden was hanged for the crime of rape. A railroad train at Madison, Fla., was boarded by about 100 persons, and two colored prisoners on their way to trial for murder were riddled with bullets. In Arkansas Frank Lane, who in a quarrel over a game of cards killed one man and fatally stabbed another, was seized by a mob, and it is supposed was taken away and lynched.

The frontier counties of Kansas, says the Chicago Tribune, have fared badly in the matter of corn-weather during August. Great areas of corn have been ruined by scorching winds and the absence of needed rain, and where the corn has not already been cut for fodder it will prove almost a total failure. In Illinois, however, the weather of the past three or four weeks has been exceptionally favorable, and the corn prospect has wonderfully improved in consequence.

Business failures throughout the country reported to New York for the week ending Aug. 26 numbered 107, a slight increase on the preceding week. Eastern States, 15; Western States, 38; Southern States, 20; Middle States, 18; Pacific States and Territories, 11; and New York city, 5.

F. D. Moulton, the purchaser of the Sprague estate at Canonchet, R. I., was driven from the property the other day by an armed band, under the instructions of the ex-Governor.

Chicago, August 28.—Richard Wilson, a shoemaker, aged 54, shot his wife this morning and then killed himself. The woman will not live. Jealousy was the cause. Seven children are left.

Prescott, August 28.—The survey for a branch road from the Atlantic and Pacific railroad to this place has been completed to Chino valley, about twenty miles from Prescott. The Atlantic and Pacific road is now within 6 miles of Williams and about 60 miles of Prescott.

Bloomington, Ill., August 28.—Prof R. B. Welch, formally principal of Pontiac school, writes from Topeka that his life is in danger from the liquor men there because as Assistant United States Attorney he has been prosecuting the violators of the State law. Within a day or two they cut his buggy in pieces and disfigured his horse and threatened his life.

Harbshaw, August 28.—News has just reached us that the Indians have murdered Mr. Martinez and two children on the Santa Cruz river, fourteen miles from this camp. Nothing further up to a lathour, except that parties bringing the news say they met two couriers on the dead run for Fort Huachuca to notify the commander. The report is considered authentic.

Toledo, O., August 28.—Excursion to Grand Rapids, 15 miles from here, on the narrow gauge road. On the return trip in the afternoon five or six desperadoes with drawn revolvers, captured the train and committed the most daring robbery and outrage. One citizen lost $75, one was thrown from the platform and a conductor was used up trying to arrest one rough. All escaped except Larry King, a notorious character whom the police secured when the train reached the city.

A Frenchman seemed to awake his especial irie and he swore to kill him before night. Happening to meet him toward evening he pulled a knife and cut the Frenchman's throat in a manner that will probably result fatally. He was seized, handcuffed and lodged in jail. A short time after the train left the mob went to the jail, took out the prisoner, and carrying him to the railroad track. hung him to one of the cross pieces of a telegraph pole. He was still hanging at a late hour this morning. Everything quiet.

After having accomplished the crime the negro fled, leaving his victim lying upon the flyor helpless. No one was present to help her in her helplessness. The father almost dumbfounded and staggering under the great blow, started at once for Odessa, about 1½ miles away, to give the alarm. ANOTHER OUTRAGE.—A Negro of Appoquinimink Commits an Unnamed Outrage upon a Little Girl.—Another of those detestable outrages called rape and which of late have become so painfully common in the lower part of New Castle co., was perpetrated by a negro on a little white girl in Appoquinimink Hundred about a mile and a half from Odaessa, on Thursday afternoon.

jim-loaf-middletown-1882-02-25.A8: THE dastardly outrage committed by "Jim" Redden upon a white girl, in the neighborhood of Odessa, is fully reported in another column. A few months ago, when William Neal, upon whom was proven a clear case of rape, was turned out unpunished upon society, it was predicted that similar outrages upon defenseless white women would speedily follow, and the predictions were well founded. The outrage is one of the most nefarious of its kind ever committed in this State, and that its perpetrator was not promptly strung up on a limb of some handy tree to kick at indefinite space, speaks strongly for the forbearance of Odessa people, and proves that they have not lost all faith in the courts of their State. The evidence against Redden seems overwhelmingly conclusive, and he will doubtless be promptly tried, convicted and executed. Should his neck be saved by such means as were resorted to in the case of the negro Neal, no remedy will be left the people for the protection of their wives and daughters but a resort to the Court of Judge Lynch.

A little more than a mile from the town of Odessa, on the road leading to Fieldsboro, and at the gate of Mr. George L. Townsend, there lives in a small one story tenement house, Henry Purse, his wife and two children. The family is poor, and Purse is much away from home at labor. The eldest child, Sarah, is a bright, intelligent girl, about 14 years old, though, being of slight stature, she does not appear to an observer to be more than thirteen. The younger child is about three years old. On Thursday afternoon of last week, whilst Purse was away at work in the neighborhood of Snyrna, and Mrs. Purse at the house of a neighbor, the two children being alone, James Redden (alias Loat), a worthless negro of notorious character, entered the house and committed a felonious outrage upon the oldest girl. The details of such crimes cannot be printed in a decent newspaper, and decent people have no desire to read them. The child was left bruised, stunned, and frightened almost out of her wits. The condition in which her mother found her upon returning home attested to the fearful manner in which she had been mal-treated by the black-hearted as well as black-skinned and beastly scoundrel. Her husband being absent, Mrs. Purse hardly knew what to do, upon first learning of the outrage, but finally decided to go to Fieldsboro and ask the advice of Henry Willard. He advised her to say nothing further of the outrage until her husband returned. Mr. Purse came home late Friday evening, but in the meantime rumors of the outrage had reached Odessa and a search was being made for the villain. The girl did not know her assailant, and a clue to his identity was obtained through Charles Bristor, a negro, who, while coming from Fieldsboro, saw Redden at a window of Purse's house. This occurred, it is believed, before the assault was committed. Obtaining this important information from Bristor, Alexander Moody and Alfred Stevens went in search of Redden, found him in front of J. G. Armstrong's store, and secured him. He was then taken to Purse's in a carriage but was not taken in the presence of Sarah until she had given a detailed description of her assailant. Redden corresponded exactly to her description, even to that of a large ring upon one of his fingers. Being taken before her she instantly recognised him as the man who had assaulted her. He was then taken back to Odessa and confined in a room in Paullin's Hotel. There was no movement to lynch him, as reported by Wilmington reporters who sat in Wilmington and wrote up the details of the affair, "hit or miss." The quiet and order-loving people of Odessa seemed to have faith that the villian would get a just amount of hanging by due process of law. Deputy Sheriff Ash Pennington went to Odessa early Saturday morning and took charge of Redden. He was taken before Esquire Vandyke, who after hearing the testimony of the victim of the outrage, and Dr. Woods, and two colored men—Bristor and Frisby Lloyd—who saw the prisoner at the house of Purse, held him for court. Ash Pennington brought him to Middletown after the hearing and took him to New Castle on the 11 o'clock train. He is now behind the bars, and, it is said, has gone to praying loudly for his soul. The reports in the Wilmington papers that an attempt was made at Middletown to lynch the villian are utterly without foundation. If Middletown people had undertaken the job they would have carried it through. Redden is a negro of notorious reputation. A few years ago he nearly killed a white boy without the least provocation, but by some means escaped punishment.

An Atrocious Crime.
One of the atrocious crimes known to the calendar, is charged to have been committed by a colored man, known as James Redden, near Odessa, Delaware, on Thursday of last week. The facts as given are as follows: Upon the day named, Redden, who also owns the alias of "Loot," visited the house of Henry Purse, on the suburbs of the village of Odessa, during the absence of all the adult members of the family.

Purse's fourteen year old daughter was at home tending the younger children when the negro arrived. After ascertaining that the girl's parents were absent, the villain caught her by the arms and, stifling her mouth, committed a beastly assault. The child's father returned, and ascertained from the neighbors that the man had been in the neighborhood, but none had guessed the repulsive nature of his errand. The girl, when questioned, related the circumstances to her father, and the news of the crime spread through the town rapidly, and the citizens were frenzied with indignation and excitement. A warrant was sworn out for Redden's arrest, and he was taken into custody while entering a store in Odessa.

THE OUTRAGED CITIZENS GATHER.

He was confined in a private house over night, and an organized band of men visited the place for the purpose of lynching the negro, but his place of concealment could not be ascertained. The next morning he was removed from the house to the depot, and but for the timely arrival of the train which carried him to New Castle jail, he would have been mobbed—the band of lynchers ran madly to the train, too late to secure the prisoner. Redden is now confined the New Castle jail, and stoutly denies the charge upon which he is held. The negro is positively identified by the outraged girl and two neighbors who saw him in the vicinity of the house. The girl suffers severely, and it is feared is seriously injured by the rufian, and the event has caused the greatest excitement in the neighborhood.

Redden is the same individual who was some time ago arrested on the charge of assaulting and badly beating a pedlar, and shortly afterward attempting to kill his own father, escaping with little or no punishment in both cases.

JAMES REDDEN PAYS THE
DEATH PENALTY OF
VIOLATED LAW.
THE CRIME.
THE CRIME.

The crime for which James Redden suffered the extreme penalty of the law was committed on the morning of the 23d of last February. His victim, little Sallie Purse, who was then about 13 years of age, being alone in the house, with the exception a baby sister, about 2 years of age. The house where the outrage was committed, is situated on the road between Odessa and Fielssboro. The father had been away for a couple of days, and the mother had gone that morning, immediately after breakfast, to see a sick person, leaving Sallie to wash the dishes and straighten up the house. About 9 o'clock Redden came along and after entering the house asked the girl to give him something to eat. Not having anything cooked she baked him some cakes, fried some meat and made some coffee. When he was done eating he went to the door and after looking up and down the road returned, and seizing hold of the child threw her on the floor, at the same time telling her "if you holler, I'll kill you," accompanying the threat with a motion as though he was about to draw a knife from his pocket.

THE ARREST.

After the foul death had been consummated he remained in the house for several hours, and then threatening her with death in case she told her mother, he took his departure. While he was in the house two colored men passed along the road and he spoke to one of them. When Mrs. Purse returned in the evening, Sallie told her what had happened but it was some time before the mother could believe it. The next day Mr. Purse returned, but before he reached home heard of the affair which by that time was pretty well known all over the country. The father had a warrant issued immediately, and Redden was arrested the same evening while holding a horse in front of Vandyke's store. He was taken to the house of Mr. Purse, and fully identified by Sallie as her assailant. The next day he was taken to New Castle where he was kept until the May term of Court when he was brought to this city for trial.

THE TRIAL AND CONVICTION.

When the case was called Harry Sharpley, Esq., was appointed by the Court to defend him. After a delay of several days, during which Mr. Sharpley was using every means in his power to obtain witnesses who would be able to clear his client of the horrid crime with which he was charged the trial was commenced.

The prisoner plead not guilty, and after some fifteen challenges had been made a jury consisting of 11 white men and 1 colored man was secured. The evidence was direct and convincing, that of his victim, who broke down several times on the stand, especially so. The defence endeavored to prove an alibi, but utterly tailed in the attempt and the few witnesses that were examined only tended to show still further that he was at the house the time the offense was committed. The counsel on both sides made able arguments, and the jury after being charged by the Chief Justice, retired at noon on the second day of the trial. The evidence was so clear that it was not expected they would be out more than a few hours, but contrary to all expectation it was 19 hours before they arrived at a verdict. They came into Court on the morning of the second day for instructions, and about an hour afterwards returned with a verdict of guilty. Immediately after the verdict was rendered Court adjourned until 3 o'clock in the afternoon. During the recess the prisoner was removed to one of the cells in the basement of the Court House, and made no hesitation in confessing his guilt and saying that all the girl had said was true.
At 3 o'clock in the afternoon of the same day he was again brought into Court and the Chief Justice after dwelling on the enormity of the crime, and picturing the blasted life of this innocent child, sentenced him to be hung on the 25th of August.

HOW HE PASSED THE TIME.

After his sentence he was removed to New Castle jail in a close carriage. He has been quiet and orderly, and ate his meals with a relish that seemed strangely in keeping with the position in which he was placed. He was frequently visited by Rev. Dr. Spotswood, a colored preacher and other friends. He learned to read and seemed to take great pleasure in reading the Bible. His mother is a constant visitor and has always tried to give him encouragement and consolation. Although she always seemed calm an observer could not fail to see that it was only by a great effort she concealed her emotions while she was in his presence. On several occasions he has confessed that he did wrong and was sorry for it.

THE EXECUTION.

Redden was executed at 10.21 this morning. The Sheriff cut the rope and his feet touched the ground. At 10.26 the movement of the heart ceased.

THE NEGRO REDDEN, WHO COMMITTED A RAPE ON A LITTLE GIRL, HANGED TO-DAY.

NEW CASTLE, DEL., August 25.—James Redden, the negro hanged here to-day for rape on a 12-year old white girl, named Sallie Purse, near Odessa, last February, passed a very restless night, praying and walking the floor, until 3 o'clock this morning, when he fell asleep and rested for an hour and a half. For breakfast he ate beef, fried eggs, bread and milk, and ice cream. He wept at times during yesterday and last night. Yesterday afternoon he was visited by two clergymen, who spent half an hour with him. His mother, who was to have visited him yesterday, failed to arrive. From 9 o'clock this morning up to the hour of his execution Redden was closeted in his cell with the Revs. Nicholas M. Brown, of New Castle, and Wesley J. Parker (colored), pastor of Ezion M. E. church, Wilmington. They prayed with him, and he joined, in a steady voice, in singing "Salvation's Free" and several other hymns. At 10:12 the prisoner, preceded by the Rev. Mr. Brown, and followed by the Rev. Mr. Parker, Warden Hance, Sheriff Clark and his son, George Clark, ascended the scaffold with a firm step and took his place on the trap. Rev. Parker offered up a short prayer, after which the noose was adjusted, the black cap drawn over the prisoner's face, his ankles pinioned and, without saying a word to those assembled, he was launched into eternity at 10:17. He died easily of strangulation in 11 minutes. The execution was witnessed only by the officers of the jail, two physicians, two clergymen, the jurors and press representatives, and one woman who manifested a strong disposition to see a man hung.

The following is a history of the case: James Redden, who was also known previous to his arrest as "Jim Loat," was a full-blooded negro, about 21 years old, and slightly under the medium stature. His face was beardless and somewhat stupid and sullen in its habitual expression. He had lived around Odessa, in the central part of this county, most all his life, and had earned a reputation for general good-for-nothingness and an ugly disposition. Besides some petty offenses, he was charged with having, some two years ago, decoyed a drunken tramp into the woods, robbed him and beaten him in a dangerous manner. On Thursday, February 231, of the present year, Redden entered the house of Henry Purse, a tenant of the late Bishop Scott, one-and-a-half miles below Odessa, during the absence of Purse and his wife, who had gone out to their daily labor learning the
entered the house of Henry Purse, a tenant of the late Bishop Scott, one-and-a-half miles below Odessa, during the absence of Purse and his wife, who had gone out to their daily labor, leaving the house in charge of their daughter Sallie, a girl of between 12 and 13 years. Sallie and her baby sister were the only inmates. The negro asked the little girl for something to eat, which she prepared and set before him. Having eaten, he lingered in the house for three hours, and during that time forcibly outraged Sallie, who resisted with all her feeble strength. But the evidence was too strong to be shaken, and the jury, after deliberating twenty-four hours, and balloting sixteen times for a verdict, found the prisoner guilty in manner and form as indicted. Redden listened to his trial and the sentence which followed close thereafter with stolic indifference, and did not seem to the observers to realize that his life had been forfeited. While awaiting his execution he maintained the same dogged indifference to his approaching doom, rarely referring to it, and still more rarely exhibiting any emotion. He was visited several times by his mother and sister, and frequently by members of the New Castle clergy, both white and colored, in whose conversation and prayers he seemed to take much comfort. He talked freely about his crime, but always stoutly maintained that it was nothing more than seduction, and that he committed no assault.

A DASTARDLY OUTBAGE.
Yesterday's Chicago papers are filled with columns of details of one of the most dastardly outrages ever perpetrated outside of Jessie James's kingdom. "From the character of the affair," says the Chicago Times, "it would seem that a section of Missouri had been brought up into Illinois and planted in Cook county. For border rufflanism it could not be equalled by New Mexican cowboys."

The facts in brief are as follows: For the past two weeks the Joliet Iron and Steel company has been taking men up from Joliet to Chicago to unload iron from the vessels at its docks in that city, and taking them home each evening. The strikers have tried to break up this sort of thing, and failed, but on Thursday evening a mob of about fifty congregated at the crossing of the Alton and Pan Handle railroads in Brighton, an outlying portion of the city, and, boarding the outgoing accommodation train, which was taking about twenty of the "scabs" home, dragged eight or ten of them from the cars and beat them shamefully, fracturing a Swede's skull and clubbing and stamping a half a dozen negroes. During the melee, which occurred inside the city limits at 5:30 in the afternoon, many shots were fired by the desperadoes. One of the bullets struck Judge N. J. Pillsbury, of Pontiac, one of the appellate judges of the Ottawa circuit, inflicting a dangerous and possibly fatal wound in the left groin. The judge was a passenger on the train, and did not leave his seat. The Judge was taken from the train to the Washington hotel where he was attended by a couple of surgeons, who found that the ball had entered at the top of the left hip, at what they called the superior spinal process of the ilium, had glanced from that bone and passed down just over the hip joint and in bedded itself in the gluteal muscles of the back. The wounded man was put under the influence of ether, and the surgeons probed for the ball but failed to find it. They did not, however, consider the wound as very dangerous, and he was able to proceed to his home by the 11 o'clock train the same night.

After the outrage was over the assailants walked away in a body leisurely, for a little distance, and then scattered like sheep, firing their revolvers as they went. They disappeared as they came, no one knowing exactly how, the engineer meantime pulling up his train to the station to enable the surgeons to remove Judge Pullsbury and the rest of the wounded. Subsequently the police made four or five arrests, but there is no certainty that any of them are the right men.

Works Attacked on a Chicago & Alton Train at Brighton Park—Three Negroes Taken from the Cars and Brutally Beaten—Judge Pillsbury Shot and Seriously Wounded.

Striking dock hands lately in the employ of the Joliet Iron & Steel Company boarded a train of the Chicago, Alton & St. Louis Railroad at Brighton Station, about five miles from this city, last evening shortly before six o'clock, and attacked a gang of "scab" laborers, white and colored, who were on their way to Joliet from Bridgeport wharf. Judge Pillsbury, of the 2d District Appellate Court, was shot seriously, if not fatally, in the groin, and three negroes and one white laborer were so terribly beaten with iron bars and stones that the recovery of at least two of them is doubtful.

The attack was planned and executed with consummate skill both as to place and time. The spot chosen is where the Alton road crosses the Pan-Handle line. All trains are compelled to halt there until the "all-right" signal has been given by the flagman. Off to the right is a Y, on which stock-yard trains change ends. From Western avenue to the railway station, perhaps 200 yards distant, the road lies through an avenue of trees thick enough to obstruct a view of the track from the adjacent houses. Moreover the road makes a short curve there. The Y is laid on a bank four feet above the bottom of the ditch, and it is believed that the conspirators hid themselves in it awaiting the approach of their victims. At all events, the telegraph operator, switchman and flagman at the crossing say they noticed no unusual number of men around until not more than five minutes before the Dwight accommodation train, which leaves the depot at Van Buren and Clark streets, was due.

As the train came in sight around the curve, the road-bed in a moment swarmed with rough-looking fellows, who, as the train halted, jumped upon the engine and presented pistols at the heads of Jones, the engineer, and the fireman and ordered them to bring the train to a dead halt. Others took position at the rear of the tender, and provided against the possibility of the train running away from them by drawing out the coupling-pin. The obnoxious seabs were known to be in the rear car, which has been attached at Bridgeport since the strikers have been resorting to violence. Into this car, by way of both doors, selected parties of the mob poured, armed with iron bars, stones and pistols. The workmen were attacked and beaten without mercy. Some who endeavored to escape through the windows and doors were assailed by the strikers, who held the track on both sides of the cars. Stones and clubs were rained upon them as they ran the gauntlet around the cars, in vain efforts to break through the lines. How any of them passed through the ordeal is the most wonderful part of it. Judge Pillsbury, who had gone into the car with a party of friends, and was playing eucher when the mob entered, arose to see what the riot was about, and had just got clear of his seat when he heard the sound of the pistol and felt the bullet. His injury was so bewildering to him and to his friends that they lost account of what was going on inside the car, remembering only the fierce yells of the infuriated assailants, and the terrified or agonized shrieks of the assailed and injured men. How long the assault lasted no one could reasonably correctly estimate. By the time the passengers in the forward cars had begun to realize what the confusion outside meant the strikers had satisfied their thirst for revenge and scattered, firing their pistols in the air by way of parting
The terrified workingmen could hardly be rallied after the mob had left. They had scattered among the gardens and houses of the vicinity, hiding in abject terror. The seriously wounded were hurt chiefly about the head, three at least having their skulls laid bare by the vicious blows. If they had been white men the strokes would undoubtedly have proved fatal. The three seriously wounded had their hurts washed and dressed as well as the rough surgery of the neighboring residents was able to do. Judge Pillsbury was carried to the station and laid on a cot. He was much prostrated by the shock and complained of numbness in his arm and leg on the side in which he was shot. Dr. Corcoran, of Albion, N. Y., happened to be on the train, and did all for him that was possible under the circumstances. Conductor Cy Adams telegraphed to police headquarters, and also to the offices of his company. A freight train just then arrived, and the caboose was detached from the train and the switch-engine on duty at the crossing attached to it. In this way Judge Pillsbury was brought to Chicago and placed in the Washington Hotel, at Madison and Canal streets.

It took the train hands forty minutes to get all the workmen together again and proceed toward Joliet. A few minutes after the train resumed its journey Lieutenant Byrne and a wagon-load of Second Precinct police arrived, but all they could do was to take note of the blood spots, with which the sides of the track were liberally spattered, and of the other marks of the conflict. All trace of the rioters was lost, and not a man of the village of Brighton or of the railway employes could be found to say that he would be able to recognize any of the assailants. All that they were willing to say they knew was that the attacking party did not attempt to disguise their features, and were total strangers to them. They gathered unseen, and were invisible as soon as they had accomplished what they came for. PITTSBURGH, June 21.—There is probably no man in the city to-day who could say more on an interesting topic than President Jarrett, of the Amalgamated Association. He has just returned from an extended and eventful trip throughout the West, has started up the Cincinnati iron works, has conferred with labor and capital in that city and St. Louis and Joliet, Ills., and Chicago and Cleveland, and places of lesser note, and reached home last evening, tired, but apparently in good humor with himself and the rest of Amalgamated mankind.

To-day Mr. Jarrett was found in the inner office of the Association, an interested spectator in the doings of the Committee on Revision. That body, with Secretary Martin, had reduced itself to shirt sleeves and absorption in the work before them. It was no place for reporters. And yet there was Mr. Jarrett with a brain as full of interesting material as is the Warren county pebble rock of oil. It was a tantalizing sight.

"I do not think it would be right to express my views of the general situation out West, or, in fact, to say anything for the press. In fact, silence is extremely golden in this case."

"The manufacturers here, Mr. Jarrett, are inclined to feel aggrieved, to say the least of it, that idle mills should start up in the wake of your recent trip."

"How about the riots at Chicago and Cleveland?"

"The trouble near Chicago was in no way chargeable to any of the members of this Association. That unfortunate affair in which Judge Pillsbury was wounded, grew out of the lawless conduct of some colored non-union iron workers from Joliet, Ill."

Murder of Miss Serena Benton.

Miss Serena J. Benton, a most worthy and respectable maiden lady, some sixty years of age, was brutally and foully murdered last Thursday morning in the broad light of day, some twenty-five steps from the public road, between the McNeil place and the Walton place, five miles west of Booneville. Miss Benton has been living in this part of the State for over forty years. She formerly taught school, supported herself and with the proceeds of her labor, bought her a farm upon which she was living, with her tenants, at the time of her death. Tuesday night of last week she staid at Mr. Bud Keistler's; Wednesday night, at Blake Davis's, all her neighbors. Thursday morning, after an early breakfast, she started to see Mr. George Michael, who had agreed to lend her some money. Mr. Michael not being at home, she left with the intention of going next to Mr. Bud Keistler's to get a book. She never reached Mr. Keistler's. On her way she passed the Walton place and was seen by Mrs. Daniel Michael as she passed. When last seen she was in the road about a hundred yards from the scene of the murder. Her not appearing at home created no uneasiness, as she was in the habit of staying several days at a time with her neighbors, so no search was made for the body. Last Monday the body was discovered by a negro, L. Simmons, who was attracted to the spot by a large number of buzzards. The neighbors soon assembled, sent for the coroner and guarded the remains all night, which were in a very thick cluster of bushes some twenty-five steps from the road. Tuesday morning we got in a buggy with Mr. George Collins and visited the place. A most horrible sight met the gaze. Language is inadequate to describe it, and we will draw the veil of silence over it. She had evidently been seized by the demons in the road and forced to the place where the murder was committed. peck-assailant-canton-1882-07.A10:
A Terrible Crime and its Reward.
Last Thursday morning, about half-past nine o'clock, we were startled by a cry for "help!" from Mr. Delano, of the Blue Store, coupled with something about Mrs. Peck, toward whose residence Mr. D. started on a run. C. W. Tetwiler, John Phoebe (colored), and one or two others followed immediately. When they reached the residence of the lady in question, they were horrified to see her struggling and screaming in the disgusting embraces of a black brute named Henry Caldwell, who had assaulted her in the yard attached to her house. Tetwiler jumped the picket fence and in the twinkling of an eye, had released the lady from the grasp of the brute. Mrs. P., a lady over sixty years of age, was assisted into her house, while Caldwell was taken into custody, though not without some trouble. He showed fight, and being very muscular would have made trouble for any one single-handed. But there were too many for him to successfully resist, and he was captured and taken at once to Judge Dinger's office, who committed him to jail to await a preliminary examination, which was held the next day. After a hearing, the evidence given being conclusive and damning to the prisoner, the Justice bound him over to the Circuit Court in the sum of $10,000.

The prisoner's "statement" before the Justice was a tissue of the most horrible falsehoods, and those present could scarcely restrain themselves from braining him as he gave it. But everything was done lawfully and in order, and he was taken to jail to await judgment at a higher tribunal.

The feelings of all classes were deeply stirred, and covert desire for a first-class lynching was general if not expressed. The delays of the law, the many loop-holes of escape, and the probable inadequacy of legal punishment were fully and freely discussed; for nothing less than death would suffice to punish the crime and serve as a deterrent to others whose "craziness" might have a bent in a similar direction.

However, Thursday and Friday nights passed without demonstration, and the idea became prevalent that the crime would be left to the arbitrament of law. Public feeling had not abated, and everybody conceded that justice as well as indemnity from this sort of crime demanded severe and summary punishment; but after the sun had twice gone down in safety to the prisoner, the chances seemed to favor his security for the present at least. But the avengers of the hideous lust of the black brute were merely biding their time.

Saturday evening, the streets were unusually quiet, being almost deserted up to eleven o'clock. Then an occasional passer-by was heard on the sidewalks of Main street. At twelve o'clock squads of two or three persons were observed, all coming toward the centre of town, and a short time after, a body of thirty or forty men had quietly assembled on the street opposite Mrs. Moser's millinery establishment. All were masked or had their faces blackened, and were otherwise disguised. There they were "sworn in," the oath administered requiring them to proceed orderly and quietly, and to forever preserve silence as to the identify of all who participated. Then they silently pursued their way to the jail.

Guards were stationed at every corner of the square on which the jail is located, and all outsiders were kept at a distance. Several parties who endeavered to get a close observation of the proceedings were warned to keep aloof, and they were discreet enough to obey the order.

The jail proper is a one-story stone building, with the jailor's residence (a two-story brick) in front and attached thereto. The entrance into the jail is made through a front door in the jailor's residence, which opens into a hall leading to the iron doors guarding the prisoners' apartments. There are two of these doors, with a narrow lobby between, and in this lobby usually sleeps Louis, a colored servant. He is somewhat of a "night
peck-assailant-canton-1882-07.A11:
owl," and on this occasion he was still out when the lynchers, headed by their captain, arrived. The front door leading to the jailor's apartments was consequently on the latch, as was also the first iron door. The second, however, was locked, as was the door of the cell in which Caldwell was confined. There were no other prisoners in the jail.

When the mob found its further progress stayed by the inner iron door, an ax was procured, and a man detailed to break the lock. The first stroke awoke the jailor, Sheriff Fletcher, who sprang from his bed on the upper story, and revolver in hand came out on the landing of the stairs to see what was the matter. A half-dozen cocked revolvars instantly covered him, and he was seized by two men, one of whom whispered in his ear: "Bill Fletcher, I am one of your best friends, but, by G—d, we're going to have that nigger!" Of course, unaided, he could do nothing, and he perforce had to let the mob have its way. Thursday and Friday nights Mr. Fletcher, fearing that something of the kind might be attempted, was prepared for such an emergency; but as two nights had passed without demonstration, and public feeling seemed to be somewhat allayed, the precautions had been omitted this night.

After hacking away at the lock in the dark ineffectually for some time, some of the men procured a lamp from the kitchen, and in a short time entrance was gained. Then the key to the cell was forcibly taken from the jailor, and in a trice the lynchers had the prisoner in their possession. A rope, with noose adjusted, was thrown over his head, and they started with him on a run for the railroad bridge. A few yells were given by some of the more excitable men as they passed the Ironton Mills, but these were quickly hushed, and no further disturbance was made until the lynching was an accomplished fact.

At the bridge the work was quickly done. The prisoner was rushed up the steps and to the centre of the bridge, when, the rope, still about his neck, was made fast to one of the projecting beams. He was then thrown over the parapet, but desperately clung to the timbers, when a slash from a knife through the muscles of his arm loosed his hold, and, dropping, he hung suspended by his neck. His feet touched the ground, however, and feeling the hanging might not be effective, some thirty shots were fired at him at short range. The suspended body was completely riddled. The crowd then gave a yell or two, and immediately dispersed, scattering in all directions.

Coroner Grandhomme was at once advised of the matter and at one o'clock in the morning he summoned a jury, went down to the bridge, received the body, cut it down, procured a coffin, and, assisted by Constable Patton and others, brought it up to the Court House, where it lay in the Sheriff's room until ten o'clock next day. Then it was taken to the potter's field and buried: and so came the end of a horrible crime and its terrible expiation.

It was not the first attempt of the kind he had made. During the past few months his actions had been such that he was forbidden to enter the premises of several families for whom he had been working, and the heads of these families had been keeping him under continual serveillance. He had imbibed the notion that he was entitled to a "white lady," and when he was arrested last Thursday, he declared that he was a man and would fight for his "rights." More than one person feels relieved to know that the brute is out of the way forever. We are not an advocate of lynch-law, but if there ever can be a case calling justly for its intervention, this was one. And that's about all we have to say about it, excepting that an example of its swift justice was needed, and to hope that the desired effect will result.

Nine-tenths of the American people, and the press of the country almost universally, have denounced this great plunder job from the start; and, when the president placed the seal of his disapprobation upon it, his patriotic action was everywhere warmly commended. sandy-bynum-huntsville-1882-08-05.A43:
AYER'S SPRINGS TRAGEDY.
Hewlett Kills Bynum.
THREE SHOTS AND INSTANT
DEATH.
The Story by Eye-Witnesses.
"Ex Deputy Marshal Hadditt
"The Story by Eye-Witnesses.

"Ex-Deputy Marshal Hewlett, accompanied by a colored man in a buggy passed our hack in which rode Sandy Bynum and others, on the Triana road some distance above Ayer's Springs going to the Barbacue, Saturday morning. He touched his hat and our crowd saluted. Shortly after arriving on the ground some one came to Bynum and told him that Hewlett was abusing him to a crowd, pointing them out standing aside from the main crowd. There were from six to seven hundred men present. Bynum went over to where Hewlett was. He was opposing the Iniependent ticket. Hewlett told Bynum that he was informed that he came down to abuse him. Bynum denied this, when Hewlett replied that he had been badly misrepresented, and if he did make personal nallusions to him in his speech he would kill him. This conversation drifted on, both parties using oaths.

Hewlett—(lifting his coat-tails and patting his hip pockets) "You see there are no pistols there."

He repeated this and walking off siad "Dont follow me." "Dont you follow me."

Sandy did not follow, and also denied having pistols, when H. returned saying angrily and with an oath: "You cant bulldoze me."—Bynum returned this, oath and all in reply, when Hewlett after turning as if to walk off, wheeled again facing his antagonist, with pistol in hand and firing instantly.

The first shot took effect in the breast and Bynum with both hands pressed against the wound whirled and while walking off in a stooping attitude received the second and third shot in lightning succession. He whirled, dropped on his back, groaned once and was dead.

Excitement was at fever heat, and cries of "Shoot him," "Kill him" went up from many parts of the ground.—Leading men, both white and colored, counseled peace and to allow the law its course. Meanwhile, displaying remarkable coolness, Hewlett reloaded the chambers of his revolver took out a second, crosed and knocked them together, saying:—"Stand back, Her, your milk. Keep off."

His horse was brought to him, which he mounted and rode off towards Triana. Up to this time his whereabouts are still unknown.

A POLITE MURDERER.
Shooting a Man and Dofling His Hat to the Spectators.
Huntsville Independent.
The siaying of Sandy Bynum, a notorious colored gambler and republican politician, by Thomas G. Hewlett, another notorious striker and ex-United States deputy marshal, at Ayer's Spring, about ten miles from Huntsville, Ala., last Saturday, has created much excitement in our county. The killing occurred at the outskirts of a crowd of between 500 and 600 colored peope. Hewlett had not dismounted from his buggy more than ten minutes and had just unhitched his splendid high-headed black mare, whose spring-gait and glossy coat had been oftentime the envy of moonshiners and their neighbors in the remotest places of Alabama. Hewlett was opposing the nongrel ticket and a small knot of colored men had gathered around him. It is stated by some that Hewlett sent for Sandy. It seems further that Hewlett cursed him, and that Sandy responded in like style. Hewlett now plunged his hand in his bosom, drew a pistol, and quick as a flash sent three balls whirling after Sandy, the first entering his breast, the second piercing his ear, and as the slain body was falling a third deadly messenger was sent after it, hitting an arm that had been raised in the agony of death.

By the time the body struck the ground life was gone. Hewlett warned every one away from him; he coolly mounted a log and proceeded to refill the empty chambers of his pistol. He said he would surrender to any one man that might be agreed upon, and would come to town and be turned over to the sheriff, but he would not give up his arms. His father was on the ground, and our informant states that Hewlett gave his father one of the pistols, as there were some indications of violence among the black people. When his black mare have been saddled he mounted her, wheeled toward the river, raised his hat to the crowd with a dare-devil mock politeness, and sped off on a lope toward the Tennessee river.

Trial of Hewlett.
The case of the State against Thomas G. Hewlett, against murder in the second degree for killing Sandy Bynum at Ayer's Springs was called up in the Circuit Court, Judge Speake presiding Tuesday morning. The defendant, accompanied by Deputy Sheriff Cooper appeared in his seat and is represented by Walker, Humes & Gordon. Solicitor Jones and Assistant Solicitor Davis and Capt. Dan Coleman Esq, represented the State. The following jury was impaneled, not however before the challenges on both sides were exhausted: W. B. Wallace, R. P. Whitman, Jas. Upton, A. B. Trewhitt, C. M. Owens, Wm. H. Webster, Walt. Laughinghouse, Jno. A. Markham, Lisn C. Blair, P. H. Strong, Jno. T. Bruce and Hiram Roberts.

The witnesses for the State and defense numbering about fifty were then sworn and put under the rule.

After the reading of the indictment, the examination of the witnesses for the State, commenced, John C. Bradley being the first placed on the stand. Next followed H. C. Binford, then John Townsend, when the court adjourned to Wednesday morning, the jury being placed under the charge of a bailiff. The examination of witnesses for the State was resumed Wednesday morning. After the testimony of Jere McDonald, B. C. Lanier Jr, John Lanier, D. D. Shelby, Dr. Shelby and others the State rested. The Defense introduced Fount Floyd, and other witnesses, the examination of which consumed the balance of the day Wednesday and all of Thursday.

The hearing of witnesses was completed Friday. Counsel on both sides waved argument and his Honor Judge Speake delivered a very clear and impartial charge to the jury, which took the case and retired about half-past three. The jury remained out Friday evening and night without returning a verdict.
